title: Office SDK vs Google Docs: a practical browser editor test
description: Run identical review, interruption, submitted-version, and export tasks before selecting a browser editor.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: Original topic reference: document platform vs Google Docs: A Working Comparison

intro: A practical Office SDK and Google Docs comparison uses the same document, roles, and delivery task in each proposed offer. The scope is an embedded Office document surface against the tested browser workspace, not an assertion that the products are feature-equivalent. Record current editions and configurations, then inspect revision behavior and recipient output when connectivity or external review interrupts the workflow.

sections.title: Choose a realistic sample
sections.html: Use a sanitized report with the structures your team needs: headings, tables, images, lists, references, and page boundaries where relevant. Include a known correction task and a required delivery format. Record the software offer, deployment configuration, browser, and test date for each candidate. Keep the original artifact unchanged and define what counts as success before beginning. A comparison should measure the same work under comparable conditions. Avoid giving one candidate a simple native document while asking another to import a complex file, unless import is specifically the requirement being assessed.

figure.title: Use one work sample from author to recipient

items.label: Author
items.detail: Perform agreed corrections in the same report sample.

items.label: Reviewer
items.detail: Verify feedback and role boundaries.

items.label: Submission
items.detail: Identify the version selected for delivery.

items.label: Recipient
items.detail: Inspect the exported file outside the platform.

figure.alt: One test follows authoring, review, submission, and external reading.
figure.caption: Keep conditions and generated outputs with the observations.

sections.title: Exercise the review relationship
sections.html: Assign author, reviewer, and viewer roles according to the organization's needs. Have the reviewer identify an issue, propose or request a change, and confirm its resolution. Test the role boundaries through direct actions as well as visible controls. Include an external participant if cross organization review matters. Measure invitation friction, comment discoverability, and whether the author can distinguish unresolved feedback from completed work. Verify current capabilities in the selected offers rather than relying on familiar behavior from another product or edition. Preserve observations that ordinary users can understand and reproduce.

sections.title: Simulate a delayed proposal
sections.html: Imagine two account managers preparing a customer proposal. One loses connectivity while the other changes the pricing explanation. Restore connectivity and inspect the resulting content, user messages, and any documented conflict behavior. Next, retrieve the version submitted before a late correction and produce the requested external file. The team should know which proposal was sent and whether subsequent editing changes that record. This scenario connects collaboration, interruption, and version clarity without assuming either candidate provides a particular offline or history capability. Record unsupported cases as explicit requirements gaps.

sections.title: Inspect output and daily effort
sections.html: Open the exported proposal in the customer's expected application and inspect page layout, tables, images, text structure, and accessibility. Ask an ordinary employee to complete the test, then count manual repairs and support interventions. Include mobile viewing, keyboard navigation, or assistive technology where required. Compare the surrounding ownership model: who stores the file, who administers access, and how retained records are recovered. An editor may meet the writing task while the overall service arrangement conflicts with operational or data handling requirements. Keep these dimensions separate in the scorecard so tradeoffs remain understandable.

sections.title: Notes from a useful test session
sections.html:
Give the tester a task sheet rather than a tour. Ask the author to correct one figure and one paragraph, ask the reviewer to verify the correction, and ask a viewer to retrieve the submitted copy. Use employees who resemble the intended users instead of relying only on platform specialists.

Task completed
Record the output or decision, not just the button pressed.
Help required
Note every administrator intervention or explanation.
Repair required
Keep before-and-after files for layout or structural repair.
Unresolved behavior
State the observed limitation and the followup needed.

In the proposal interruption test, do not assume any particular offline capability. Record what remains editable, what message appears, when work is acknowledged, and what happens after reconnection. Compare the final content with the intended edits from both authors. Then identify the version submitted to the customer and inspect the external file. This yields a concrete description of the tested workflow rather than a claim that one editor is universally better. If a result changes after a release or configuration adjustment, update the test record with the new conditions.

figure.title: Record what ordinary users actually needed

items.label: Completion
items.detail: Which task and output were successfully finished?

items.label: Assistance
items.detail: Which explanation or administrator action was required?

items.label: Repair
items.detail: What had to be changed after export?

items.label: Constraint
items.detail: What remains unsupported or unverified?

figure.alt: Four observation categories distinguish task success from demonstration fluency.
figure.caption: Use observed evidence when making the selection recommendation.

sections.title: Comparison Decision notes
sections.html:
• Use the same sample, instructions, and required output for both candidates.
  • Verify author, reviewer, viewer, and guest boundaries.
  • Test interruption and identification of the submitted version.
  • Inspect exported files in the actual recipient application.
  • Record user time, repairs, support work, and ownership constraints.

title: Private cloud Google Docs alternatives: network and data tests
description: Translate private deployment requirements into separate editing, network, dependency, and maintenance checks.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: Original topic reference: Self-Hosted Google Docs Alternative for Private Deployment

intro: A private cloud Google Docs alternative must pass both the writing task and the deployment boundary. Specify permitted processing, administration, and outbound dependencies, then trace source retrieval, saved state, and export. Installation location alone does not establish independence or acceptable data handling.

sections.title: State the boundary and test both halves
sections.html:
Define the hosting environment, permitted networks, administration model, and any restrictions on external communication. A private cloud might mean an isolated virtual network, dedicated infrastructure, or an internally operated service; those arrangements have different implications. Identify whether licensing, telemetry, updates, or support require outbound connectivity. Confirm the exact edition's documented requirements and inspect network behavior in a controlled test. Record where document bytes, editing state, logs, and backups reside. The requirement should describe permitted processing and access, not merely the location of the web application container.

Use one test set for authoring, collaboration, comments, versions, and required exports, and another for identity, network access, recovery, and maintenance. This prevents an excellent editing demonstration from masking an unsupported deployment requirement. It also prevents a successful installation from being mistaken for satisfactory document fidelity. Test the actual file structures and simultaneous use expected by the organization. For the private deployment set, verify certificate trust, source retrieval, callbacks, and storage access from the components that perform those requests. A link reachable in an administrator's browser may be unreachable to a conversion worker.

figure.title: Private deployment includes data and administration paths

items.label: User access
items.detail: Internal identity and approved browser routes.

items.label: Processing
items.detail: Editing, conversion, and source retrieval.

items.label: Persistence
items.detail: Objects, state, logs, and recovery data.

items.label: Administration
items.detail: Updates, licensing, support, and privileged access.

figure.alt: Four paths must fit the intended private deployment boundary.
figure.caption: A local container verifies only a small part of this arrangement.

sections.title: Work through an isolated research team
sections.html:
Suppose a research institute needs collaborative drafting inside a restricted network. Staff use the internal identity system, documents originate in a protected repository, and approved reports are exported for publication. Deploy a candidate in a representative environment and trace the first open, collaborative changes, saved state, and export. Then block unauthorized outbound destinations and inspect failures. Determine whether the supported architecture still operates and which update or support processes require an approved transfer route. Use synthetic documents for these tests so network troubleshooting does not expose unpublished research to an unintended destination.

Test the boundary under failure, not only when everything works. A source retrieval error might trigger support diagnostics; a parser crash might create an attachment containing document bytes; a failed license check might require an external recovery step. Inspect the supported behavior and approved routes for these cases.

StageBoundary questionEvidence
First openWhich component retrieves the source?Safe request trace from that component
ProcessingWhere do conversion and editing state run?Deployment and observed network path
FailureWhere do diagnostics and temporary files go?Controlled failure inspection
MaintenanceHow do updates and support enter the boundary?Rehearsed approved procedure

For the research institute, disable unauthorized destinations and run a representative task plus a staged failure. Record which functions remain available and which need a supported alternative. An undocumented workaround is a risk to assign and resolve. If the organization accepts an external dependency, state its purpose and conditions precisely rather than keeping an overly broad claim that the entire service is isolated.

sections.title: Assign continuing operational work
sections.html: Private deployment transfers or changes responsibilities for patching, backups, monitoring, certificates, capacity, and incident response. Name an owner for each and compare the workload with available staffing. Rehearse a release upgrade, a failed storage request, and restoration of both content and permission metadata. Establish a supported escalation arrangement and clarify whether supplier diagnostics require document access. Include infrastructure and maintenance effort in cost estimates. The operating plan should also explain how files and relevant metadata can be exported if the deployment is retired, preventing an internal service from becoming an undocumented permanent dependency.

figure.title: Evaluate writing and deployment as separate gates

items.label: Writing gate
items.detail: Real documents, review, and export pass.

items.label: Boundary gate
items.detail: Processing, access, and dependencies fit policy.

items.label: Operations gate
items.detail: Assigned staff can update and recover the service.

figure.alt: Three gates assess functional, boundary, and operating suitability.
figure.caption: A pass in one gate does not compensate for an unresolved mandatory gate.

sections.title: Private deployment Decision notess
sections.html:
• Define hosting, network, processing, and administrative boundaries.
  • Verify outbound dependencies for the exact supported offer.
  • Run separate editing and deployment acceptance suites.
  • Trace source retrieval, saved state, export, and recovery.
  • Assign maintenance owners and confirm escalation and exit arrangements.

title: Document data sovereignty: map processing, access, and law
description: Separate storage residency, processing locations, legal access, and operational control in a document workflow.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: Original topic reference: Data Sovereignty in Document Collaboration

intro: Document data sovereignty involves processing locations, operators, legal arrangements, and administrative control as well as storage residency. Map the complete information path and have responsible specialists assess the relevant requirements. A bucket in the selected region does not establish the position of every document copy or operator.

sections.title: Separate the questions being asked
sections.html: Identify whether the requirement concerns residency, international transfers, legal jurisdiction, operational control, or continuity under supplier disruption. These questions overlap but are not interchangeable. A local data center can host a service administered from abroad, and a locally operated service can send conversion jobs to an external endpoint. Work with legal and security owners to translate the organization's obligations into technical requirements. Document which data classes and workflows are in scope. Avoid a blanket statement that all information is sovereign when only the primary storage bucket's region has been verified.

figure.title: Sovereignty questions span four boundaries

items.label: Storage
items.detail: Objects, caches, logs, and backups have locations.

items.label: Processing
items.detail: Workers and optional services handle document data.

items.label: Administration
items.detail: Operators, keys, and support paths control access.

items.label: Legal arrangement
items.detail: Responsible specialists assess contracts and obligations.

figure.alt: Four boundaries require different kinds of evidence.
figure.caption: Keep technical observations distinguishable from legal assessment.

sections.title: Trace the complete processing path
sections.html: Follow a document from upload through editing, preview generation, search indexing, export, backup, and support investigation. Record each processing location, operator, and permitted access route. Include metadata and logs because they may reveal sensitive business activity even without full file contents. Inspect optional integrations separately, especially analytics and AI services. For each connection, identify purpose, destination, authentication, retention, and governing arrangement. Verify current deployment behavior with network and configuration evidence where practical. Architecture diagrams should be updated when a new feature introduces a worker, cache, or remote service into the information path.

sections.title: Use a cross border project example
sections.html: Imagine an infrastructure project involving domestic engineers and an overseas consultant. The contract restricts certain design records to approved locations but allows a sanitized review package to be shared. Create separate workflows for internal collaboration and permitted external disclosure. Test which artifacts and metadata cross the boundary during invitation, preview, export, and support. Confirm who approves each disclosure and how access ends after the engagement. The arrangement may require contractual and legal analysis beyond a technical setting. Keep those decisions linked to the actual file classification and deployment paths instead of relying on a generic guest sharing policy.

sections.title: Inspect administrative independence
sections.html: Determine who holds encryption keys, privileged credentials, backup access, and the ability to change processing destinations. Review supplier support procedures and any exceptional access path. Ask how the service continues if a license server, update channel, or remote operator becomes unavailable. These are operational questions alongside legal ones, and their answers vary by offer and architecture. Test recovery and export within the permitted boundary. A deployment that stores files locally but cannot restore or update without unauthorized external access may not satisfy the organization's intended control requirement.

sections.title: Ask four different location questions
sections.html:
QuestionWhat to inspectWhat it does not establish
Where are files stored?Primary objects, caches, logs, and backupsWhere every computation runs
Where are files processed?Editing, conversion, indexing, and AI pathsWho may administer the system
Who can access them?Privileged roles, support, and key ownershipApplicable legal interpretation
Which arrangements apply?Operators, contracts, and assessed legal obligationsActual network behavior

For the infrastructure project, create one map for internal design records and another for the sanitized review package. Include metadata shared with the consultant, not only the exported drawing. The two workflows may have different approved boundaries, and the decision should make that difference explicit.

When the architecture changes, compare the new path against the accepted map. A new preview service, AI plugin, or remote support mechanism may change processing or access even if the primary storage location stays the same. Assign a review trigger to those changes. Preserve configuration and observations as technical evidence, while marking contractual or legal conclusions as decisions of the responsible specialists. This prevents the system diagram from claiming more than it can prove.

figure.title: An approved external review package has its own path

items.label: Classify
items.detail: Identify restricted design records.

items.label: Prepare
items.detail: Create the permitted sanitized package.

items.label: Approve
items.detail: Owner authorizes the scope and recipient.

items.label: Disclose
items.detail: Use the approved route and record the version.

items.label: Close
items.detail: Review expiry and terminate engagement access.

figure.alt: Classification and approval precede disclosure of an identified package.
figure.caption: Do not broaden the internal workflow's boundary through an ad hoc export.

sections.title: Sovereignty assessment Decision notes
sections.html:
• State the precise residency, transfer, jurisdiction, and control requirements.
  • Map content, metadata, processing, backups, and support access.
  • Assess each operator and contractual arrangement with responsible specialists.
  • Test approved external disclosure and blocked transfer cases.
  • Verify key ownership, recovery, updates, and service continuity assumptions.

title: Self hosted collaboration: an operating plan for the first month
description: Establish service ownership, document acceptance, pilot support, restoration, and rollout evidence.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: Original topic reference: A Practical Guide to Self-Hosted Collaboration

intro: The first month of self hosted collaboration should establish a supported service: named owners, complete document tests, a bounded pilot, and a demonstrated recovery path. Schedule those outcomes rather than measuring progress only by installation steps. Expansion needs evidence that ordinary users and operators can do their jobs.

sections.title: Week one: define the service
sections.html: Assign business, application, infrastructure, identity, and support owners. Write the intended workload, supported file types, required integrations, availability expectations, and recovery targets. Use the product's current deployment documentation to establish prerequisites and supported topology. Record certificate, database, storage, network, and licensing responsibilities. Make the document lifecycle explicit: who stores source files, how first opening works, where active editing state lives, and how results return to the business application. A short service description with named owners prevents the installation from becoming a collection of components that nobody is accountable for as a whole.

sections.title: Week two: test complete workflows
sections.html: Prepare sanitized documents representing normal and difficult work. Test creation or import, first open, collaborative edits, saved state, download, and reopening. Include denied access, expired credentials, unsupported files, and an unavailable source endpoint. Observe failures from the requesting component's network rather than relying only on an administrator's browser. Record acceptance results with correlation identifiers and safe logs. Check that users receive understandable states when conversion or export is still processing. Resolve contract ambiguities such as what Saved means before the pilot starts, because support staff need consistent explanations for these milestones.

figure.title: The first month creates four verifiable outcomes

items.label: Service definition
items.detail: Owners, lifecycle, workload, and recovery expectations.

items.label: Acceptance
items.detail: Complete workflows and meaningful failures are tested.

items.label: Pilot
items.detail: Users finish work; support follows the runbook.

items.label: Operations
items.detail: Restoration and maintenance are demonstrated.

figure.alt: Four stage outcomes support controlled expansion.
figure.caption: Calendar dates help coordinate the work; gates determine readiness.

sections.title: Week three: run a bounded pilot
sections.html: Choose a team with meaningful but manageable work, such as a procurement group preparing weekly supplier reports. Keep a clear route to the previous workflow during the pilot. Train users on the specific business tasks and tell them where to report incidents. Measure task completion, startup delays, failed exports, administrator interventions, and recurring confusion. Have support staff diagnose one staged failure using the runbook rather than asking the original engineer directly. The pilot should establish whether the service is operable by its intended team, not merely whether enthusiastic early users can work around problems.

sections.title: Week four: rehearse operation
sections.html:
Restore a backup into an isolated environment and verify documents, identities, permissions, and integration mappings. Apply a supported update in staging and record the maintenance steps and rollback limits. Confirm monitoring for user facing failures, queue delays, storage errors, and certificate expiry. Agree on incident severity, escalation, and communication ownership. Review pilot findings with business owners and decide which gaps must be resolved before expansion. Add capacity based on measured workloads rather than extrapolating from user account counts. Keep configuration and runbooks in a maintainable location with access for the responsible operators.

The four-week schedule is a planning aid, not permission to move on with an unresolved dependency. Give each stage an exit condition and a named reviewer. If source retrieval still fails intermittently, a pilot deadline does not make the problem acceptable by itself.

  1. Service gate: owners agree on lifecycle, workload, recovery targets, and support boundaries.
  2. Workflow gate: representative files complete first open, editing, save, export, and reopen.
  3. Pilot gate: ordinary users finish agreed tasks and support staff diagnose a staged failure.
  4. Operations gate: operators demonstrate restoration and the supported update procedure.

For the procurement pilot, select a weekly report with a workbook and narrative document. Measure completion and failures at the user task level, then correlate them with service observations. If reports complete only because the installer intervenes each Friday, the pilot has exposed an ownership or automation gap.

At the expansion review, record accepted limitations and their consequences. A file type outside the agreed scope should have a clear user route, while a failed core save path needs correction before broader use. Keep issues as concrete owned work, with the evidence needed to close each one. This makes the next wave a deliberate service decision rather than an automatic date on a rollout calendar.

figure.title: Can the service expand beyond the pilot?

items.label: Expand
items.detail: Core tasks pass and operators can recover the service.

items.label: Hold
items.detail: A mandatory task or ownership gap remains unresolved.

items.label: Bounded exception
items.detail: Owner accepts a specific limit with a documented route.

figure.alt: Expansion, hold, or a bounded exception requires an explicit decision.
figure.caption: Tie the decision to observed tasks and assigned operating capability.

sections.title: Next wave readiness
sections.html:
• Confirm owners, workload, recovery targets, and supported architecture.
  • Pass complete document workflows and meaningful failure cases.
  • Review pilot completion rates and support interventions.
  • Demonstrate backup restoration and a supported maintenance procedure.
  • Assign remaining issues and establish a controlled expansion schedule.

title: Private cloud collaboration: who operates and owns each part?
description: Write a responsibility model for infrastructure, document state, privileged access, maintenance, and recovery.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: Original topic reference: Private Cloud Document Collaboration: Self-Hosted Guide

intro: Private cloud collaboration needs a responsibility model that identifies infrastructure ownership, service operators, data authority, and privileged access. Specify who patches, monitors, backs up, restores, and verifies the service. A dedicated environment does not eliminate shared responsibilities or guarantee that somebody owns every operating task.

sections.title: Describe the actual arrangement
sections.html: State where infrastructure runs, who owns the account or hardware, who deploys software, and who can administer the service. Identify whether resources are dedicated or logically separated and what isolation evidence is required. List external dependencies such as licensing, update repositories, support access, and optional processing services. Confirm the exact product offer supports the intended architecture. A private network address does not prove that every document operation stays inside the network. Trace data paths and administrative paths separately, because the ability to change configuration or retrieve a backup can matter as much as routine application access.

sections.title: Assign document authority
sections.html: Identify the system that owns each stage of the lifecycle: original files, active editing state, published business versions, and retained records. If several services are involved, document identifiers and handoff rules. Specify who authorizes creation, export, sharing, and deletion. A private cloud deployment can still have ambiguous ownership when an editor's durable state and the business application's downloadable file differ. Define the visible saved milestone and the authoritative version returned to users. Include reconciliation procedures for interrupted exports or callbacks so the system can recover without silently presenting stale content as current.

figure.title: A private deployment has separate authority layers

items.label: Infrastructure
items.detail: Account, network, storage, and hardware ownership.

items.label: Service operation
items.detail: Deployment, monitoring, updates, and incidents.

items.label: Document authority
items.detail: Business IDs, saved states, and published versions.

items.label: Privileged access
items.detail: Approved support and administration routes.

figure.alt: Four authority layers identify the parties involved in a deployment.
figure.caption: Private hosting describes the arrangement; these layers describe responsibility.

sections.title: Test a managed deployment example
sections.html: Suppose an organization uses its own cloud account while a supplier operates the collaboration service. The organization manages identity and data classification; the supplier manages releases and infrastructure incidents. Write a responsibility table for backups, certificate rotation, support access, security updates, capacity, and recovery verification. Then stage a storage outage and observe which party detects it, communicates impact, restores access, and confirms document integrity. The exercise often reveals tasks assigned vaguely to both parties or to neither. Convert those gaps into named ownership and response expectations before production approval.

sections.title: Control privileged and change access
sections.html: Use attributable administrator identities and an approved process for exceptional access to document content. Define how supplier access is granted, limited, logged, and revoked. Protect service credentials and encryption keys according to the agreed responsibility model. For releases, require supported versions, change records, staging results, and understood rollback limits. Test restoration with the party that will perform it during an incident, including required metadata and permissions. Review the operating arrangement when staff, suppliers, or account ownership changes. A responsibility model that is never updated can become less accurate than the undocumented practice it was meant to replace.

sections.title: Separate execution from accountability
sections.html:
A task can be executed by a supplier while the organization remains accountable for its requirement. Keep both roles visible. For restoration, the supplier might run the procedure, the infrastructure team might supply the isolated target environment, and the business owner might verify that the restored version is the right one.

TaskExecutor to nameDecision owner to name
Backup jobOperator of the relevant durable storeOwner of recovery policy
Release updateMaintainer of the deploymentOwner approving business impact
Support accessAuthorized investigatorOwner approving scope and conditions

sections.title: Test the responsibility gaps
sections.html:
Stage a failure that crosses the organizational boundary. For example, storage rejects exports while editing sessions remain available. Ask who notices the delayed business versions, who opens the incident, who investigates credentials, and who tells users which saved state is safe.

Record any task answered with We assumed they handled it. Convert that assumption into an assigned role, an escalation route, and a verification step. Also test the opposite problem: both parties independently restart or reconfigure the same service. Shared involvement needs coordination, especially when a retry can publish a new version. The exercise should leave an operating agreement that matches how the parties will actually respond under pressure.

figure.title: A storage failure tests the shared operating model

items.label: Detection
items.detail: Identify the stalled export or unavailable object.

items.label: Triage
items.detail: Assigned owner correlates the service and storage paths.

items.label: Recovery
items.detail: Authorized executor applies the agreed procedure.

items.label: Verification
items.detail: Business owner checks version, content, and permissions.

figure.alt: A failure needs detection, triage, recovery, and business verification.
figure.caption: Assign an owner at each handoff before the service goes live.

sections.title: Responsibility model Decision notes
sections.html:
• Identify infrastructure ownership, operators, isolation, and external dependencies.
  • Assign authority for content states and lifecycle transitions.
  • Name owners for backup, updates, monitoring, certificates, and incidents.
  • Test a failure across organizational boundaries.
  • Verify privileged access records and periodic responsibility reviews.

title: Presentation version history: recover the deck actually sent
description: Keep milestones, source provenance, comparisons, and distribution records so deck history answers real questions.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: OfficeDex: Every deck has a history. OfficeDex lets you walk back into it

intro: Useful presentation history identifies the deck that was reviewed, sent, or presented, together with the source data behind important claims. Autosave timestamps alone are not enough. Preserve meaningful milestones and compare data changes separately from layout so historical figures and decisions remain explainable.

sections.title: Distinguish checkpoints from milestones
sections.html: Frequent editing checkpoints protect work, while named milestones capture business meaning such as Reviewed by finance or Sent to the customer. Keep both where the chosen tooling permits, but do not make users infer a submission from the newest timestamp. Tie a milestone to the exact deck content and relevant attachments. Assign stable slide identities if the implementation needs comparisons across reordering or duplication. A slide's position is a weak identifier because inserting an agenda changes every subsequent number. Define retention and deletion policies for history, particularly when previous decks contain sensitive figures or superseded statements.

figure.title: Identify which deck mattered at each milestone

items.label: Review
items.detail: Named reviewers accept an exact version.

items.label: Send
items.detail: Record the file actually distributed.

items.label: Present
items.detail: Identify any different displayed copy.

items.label: Successor
items.detail: Continue work without changing the historical record.

figure.alt: Review, distribution, presentation, and later work are distinct milestones.
figure.caption: Use these distinctions where they matter to the business task.

sections.title: Capture enough provenance
sections.html: Record which datasets, documents, prompts, or manual inputs contributed to important slides. For generated content, preserve the task specification and review outcome at a level appropriate to confidentiality and reproducibility. Do not assume that saving a prompt makes later generation identical; models and surrounding tools can change. For numerical claims, preserve the source version or extraction date and any transformation logic. A chart whose data has moved on may still be correct for a historical meeting. Provenance helps reviewers distinguish an outdated deck from an accurate record of what was known at the time.

sections.title: Reconstruct an investor meeting
sections.html: Imagine a team revising an investor presentation the night before a meeting. Finance changes a revenue chart, legal adjusts a disclaimer, and the presenter simplifies the narrative. Mark the final reviewed deck and separately record the version actually distributed. A week later, a director asks why the growth figure differs from the current dashboard. Retrieve the sent deck, its source data date, and the chart calculation. This scenario requires content and provenance together. Restoring the newest editable deck alone may not reproduce the material the audience saw or the evidence behind its claims.

sections.title: Compare changes meaningfully
sections.html: Useful comparisons distinguish text edits, layout changes, chart data changes, and slide additions or removals. Inspect the chosen product's actual history and comparison features before designing around them. If comparisons are built externally, preserve both semantic structure and rendered previews where practical. Rendering can show visual differences, while structured data explains changed values or references. Avoid presenting a layout only change as equivalent to a changed financial claim. When restoring a prior version, create a clear new working state and protect later submissions from accidental replacement. Record who initiated restoration and what happened to subsequent edits.

sections.title: The sent deck is a separate record
sections.html:
In the investor meeting scenario, the final reviewed deck and the distributed deck may be identical, but verify that rather than assuming it. A presenter can make a last-minute change after review or attach the wrong file. Record distribution against the actual artifact using a version identifier and, where useful, an integrity digest.

Reviewed milestone
The version accepted by the named reviewers.
Sent milestone
The exact artifact delivered to the audience.
Presented milestone
The version displayed, if different from the distributed copy.
Working successor
The current editable deck prepared for later use.

These are proposed record distinctions; assess what the chosen tools can capture. If the platform cannot record distribution, the surrounding business process may need to do it.

For a questioned growth chart, retrieve its source period and transformation before comparing it with today's dashboard. The historical deck may be accurate for the data available then. If the chart was wrong, create an identified correction and preserve the earlier record according to policy. Overwriting it can make it impossible to explain what the audience saw. A history reconstruction should produce both the visual artifact and enough provenance to interpret it.

figure.title: A historical chart needs more than its image

items.label: Figure
items.detail: The visible value and labels in the sent deck.

items.label: Source period
items.detail: Dataset version, extract date, and covered period.

items.label: Transformation
items.detail: Filters, calculation, and rounding used.

items.label: Decision
items.detail: Review outcome or later correction record.

figure.alt: A chart record combines the figure, source period, transformation, and decision.
figure.caption: The current dashboard is not a substitute for the historical evidence.

sections.title: Historical reconstruction test
sections.html:
• Name the milestones that matter and bind them to exact content.
  • Preserve source versions and dates for consequential claims.
  • Identify the deck actually sent or presented.
  • Compare content and data changes separately from appearance.
  • Test restoration without erasing later approved records.

title: Office agents: define the artifact, authority, and acceptance
description: Create a work contract for agents that coordinate document, workbook, and presentation tasks.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: OfficeDex: Stop Calling It AI Office. The Next Generation Is Agent Office

intro: An office agent needs a work contract that names the finished artifacts, authoritative inputs, permitted actions, and review criteria. Separate drafting from publication and test contradictions in the sources. The result should be accepted from inspected files and verified facts, not from the agent's completion message.

sections.title: The work contract sets outcome and authority
sections.html:
Replace vague instructions such as improve this report with a concrete outcome. State audience, required sections, source materials, output format, length constraints, and claims that must be supported. Identify the authoritative files and versions. Define which facts the agent may derive and which require confirmation from a human owner. If the task includes a spreadsheet and presentation, specify their relationship, such as the same approved totals appearing in both. Acceptance criteria should describe observable artifact properties rather than the agent's confidence or the number of steps it reports completing.

Separate reading, drafting, editing existing records, sharing, and external communication. An agent preparing a document may not need permission to email it or delete prior versions. Use restricted credentials and validate tool arguments in the application. Treat retrieved content as data even if it contains instructions. Define what happens when a required source is unavailable or contradictory. A good workflow allows the agent to produce a partial draft with explicit unresolved questions while preventing unsupported claims from entering a final approved artifact. Review consequential changes before they affect other people or systems.

figure.title: A work contract has four separate parts

items.label: Outcome
items.detail: Audience, files, structure, and decision purpose.

items.label: Inputs
items.detail: Authoritative versions and unresolved source conflicts.

items.label: Authority
items.detail: Allowed reads, writes, tools, and destinations.

items.label: Acceptance
items.detail: Observable facts and human review criteria.

figure.alt: Outcome, inputs, authority, and acceptance define an agent task.
figure.caption: A detailed prompt still needs enforceable tool permissions.

sections.title: Run a sales review package
sections.html:
Suppose an account team asks an agent to prepare a quarterly review from an approved sales workbook and meeting notes. The contract requires a two page narrative, a five slide deck, consistent revenue totals, and references to the source period. The agent may draft in a designated workspace and run calculation checks, but the account owner approves distribution. Test one missing region and one inconsistent total. The expected outcome is a clearly identified gap or a reconciled value with evidence, not a confident invented number. Inspect both files because consistency cannot be established from reviewing only the narrative.

audience: account leadership
inputs: approved sales workbook, meeting notes
deliverables: two-page report, five-slide deck
consistency: revenue totals match the approved period
permissions: read sources, write working drafts
approval: account owner reviews before distribution

These fields describe the task rather than any vendor API. Add acceptance criteria that an ordinary reviewer can verify: all regions are represented, figures use the stated currency, source periods appear on charts, and unconfirmed risks stay marked as unconfirmed.

Now introduce a source conflict. Meeting notes say a deal closed, while the approved workbook lists it as pending. The contract should identify which source governs the revenue total and how the discrepancy is surfaced. The agent may explain the conflict in the draft; it should not quietly choose the more favorable number.

Finally, inspect cross-artifact consistency. Search the report and deck for the affected deal and total. A corrected workbook lookup does not prove that generated narrative and chart labels were updated. Keep the accepted output versions with the review outcome. If a run is interrupted, a new attempt should produce or resume a clearly identified working state rather than duplicate the final package or distribute an unreviewed successor.

sections.title: Make progress and recovery observable
sections.html: Record task state, source versions, generated artifacts, tool actions, and human decisions. Give users a way to cancel a run and understand whether any changes were already applied. If a step fails, retries should not create duplicate submissions or overwrite newer edits. Use version checks and idempotent publication where the architecture supports them. Separate temporary working files from approved outputs and clean them up according to policy. The agent's visible progress should refer to verifiable milestones such as Draft created or Totals checked, rather than implying that all downstream work is complete.

figure.title: Conflicting input should remain visible in the draft

items.label: Conflict
items.detail: Notes call a deal closed; approved data says pending.

items.label: Rule
items.detail: Use the nominated source for revenue totals.

items.label: Draft
items.detail: Flag the discrepancy without inventing a resolution.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Owner resolves it and checks every output.

figure.alt: A source conflict follows an explicit rule and human resolution.
figure.caption: Verify the report, deck, and any related workbook together.

sections.title: Contract Decision notes Decision notes reuse
sections.html:
• Specify audience, artifact structure, source versions, and supported claims.
  • Limit tool authority and define required human decisions.
  • Test missing inputs, contradictions, and hostile source instructions.
  • Inspect every output and verify cross artifact consistency.
  • Confirm cancellation, safe retries, and approved publication behavior.

title: Connected reports: freshness, refresh failures, and publication
description: Set source version, validation, stale-data behavior, and fixed publication rules for connected reports.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: OfficeDex: Keep Reports Current with Connected Data

intro: A connected report needs a freshness contract: which source period it represents, when it refreshes, what validation runs, and what happens if a feed fails. Keep live working data separate from approved publications. Refreshing a chart does not automatically update the conclusion written beside it.

sections.title: Specify the freshness promise
sections.html: Choose whether the report shows live values, the latest validated extract, or an approved period end snapshot. These are different products and should have different labels. Record the source system, relevant time zone, extraction time, covered period, and known delays. A report refreshed at noon can still contain data posted only through yesterday. Define the maximum acceptable age and what users see when that threshold is exceeded. Avoid displaying a generic Updated message that refers only to page generation while the underlying dataset remains stale. Freshness must describe the data the audience is actually reading.

sections.title: Own the transformation logic
sections.html: Document joins, filters, calculations, rounding, and mappings between source fields and displayed values. Assign an owner who can explain and review that logic. Validate schema changes, missing categories, duplicate records, and unexpected totals before updating the report. When several artifacts reuse the same numbers, use a common validated dataset or clearly defined transformation rather than separate manual formulas. Keep data access credentials scoped to the required source and operation. A report generator should not need broad write access merely because it reads a sales database. Log refresh outcomes without unnecessarily copying sensitive records into diagnostic output.

figure.title: Refresh does not equal publication

items.label: Extract
items.detail: Read an identified source period or snapshot.

items.label: Validate
items.detail: Check schema, completeness, totals, and transformations.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Verify commentary still matches the figures.

items.label: Publish
items.detail: Bind the output to the accepted data version.

figure.alt: Extraction, validation, narrative review, and publication are distinct.
figure.caption: Keep historical publications fixed unless issuing an identified correction.

sections.title: Test a weekly operations report
sections.html: Imagine a delivery team generating a weekly report with shipment counts, delays, and customer impact. On Monday, one source feed arrives late and a region changes its status code. The refresh should identify incomplete or unmapped data instead of silently dropping rows. Decide whether to hold publication, retain the last validated dataset with a warning, or publish a labeled partial report. Review both numbers and narrative commentary: a sentence claiming delays fell may become false when refreshed values show an increase. Connected charts do not automatically update the reasoning surrounding them, so commentary needs its own validation.

sections.title: Separate refresh from publication
sections.html: A working report can refresh repeatedly while an approved report remains fixed. At publication, bind the artifact to the validated data version and retain its generation metadata. If a correction is needed, issue a new identified edition rather than silently altering the record already distributed. Test refresh failures, overlapping jobs, and retries so an older result cannot replace a newer validated state. Where data links require the reader's access, define behavior for recipients who lack permission. The final artifact should either contain the agreed snapshot or clearly explain why live content cannot be loaded.

sections.title: Choose a stale-data behavior explicitly
sections.html:
When a source is late, choose a behavior that matches the report's purpose. Holding publication can be appropriate for a formal operating pack. Keeping the last validated dataset may be appropriate for a working dashboard if its age is obvious. A partial report needs a clear scope label and a decision about whether the audience can safely use it.

BehaviorReader must know
HoldThe expected publication is not ready
Last validatedThe data period and age of the retained values
PartialWhich regions or categories are missing

sections.title: A refresh result needs four timestamps
sections.html:
Source coverage
The period represented by the records.
Extraction
When the source snapshot was read.
Validation
When completeness and transformation checks passed.
Publication
When the identified report became available.

For the weekly delivery report, a Monday publication may contain a Friday extract with Sunday source coverage, depending on the system's posting behavior. Use accurate labels for the actual arrangement rather than letting one Updated time imply all four. After replacing a late region's values, recheck totals and commentary. A statement about falling delays can become false even when every chart refreshed successfully. Preserve the dataset version used for the published edition so corrections can be explained.

figure.title: A late source feed needs a defined response

items.label: Hold publication
items.detail: Explain that the required complete report is not ready.

items.label: Keep validated data
items.detail: Show its period and age clearly.

items.label: Publish partial
items.detail: Identify missing scope and the permitted use.

figure.alt: Three degraded behaviors have different implications for readers.
figure.caption: Choose the behavior with the business owner before a failure occurs.

sections.title: Refresh Decision notes Decision notes
sections.html:
• State whether values are live, validated, or fixed at publication.
  • Label data period, extraction time, and acceptable age.
  • Validate schema, completeness, totals, and narrative consistency.
  • Define degraded behavior for late feeds and failed refreshes.
  • Bind published outputs to a retained data version.

title: Editable AI PowerPoint: inspect objects before accepting the deck
description: Verify editable charts, text, diagrams, themes, and the next real revision in the recipient application.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: OfficeDex: An editable AI PowerPoint checklist for everyday work

intro: An editable AI PowerPoint deck should let the team change the objects that matter: text, figures, chart data, diagrams, and branding. Inspect the exported file and perform the next revision task. A presentation file extension and an attractive preview do not establish practical editability.

sections.title: Define required editability
sections.html: List the changes the team expects to make after generation: update a title, replace a figure, change chart values, move a diagram node, apply the brand theme, or translate a slide. A background image may be acceptable for decoration but unsuitable for a chart that changes weekly. Specify which elements must be native editable objects and which may remain raster images. Inspect the actual exported presentation rather than assuming an editable format guarantees editable content. Also identify the target applications and versions, because a deck's usability can differ when opened in the recipient's environment.

figure.title: Inspect the objects that future editors must change

items.label: Text
items.detail: Selectable text with sensible grouping and reading order.

items.label: Charts
items.detail: Required values, series, and labels are editable.

items.label: Diagrams
items.detail: Shapes and connectors support the intended revision.

items.label: Layouts
items.detail: Theme and placeholders support reuse.

figure.alt: Four object families determine the deck's practical editability.
figure.caption: Inspect the exported file in the target application.

sections.title: Inspect structure and data
sections.html: Select text and shapes individually, check grouping, and verify that reading order makes sense. For charts, inspect whether the underlying values can be edited and whether labels match the source data. Confirm that diagrams contain manageable objects rather than hundreds of fragmented paths or one flat image. Review fonts, theme colors, slide masters, and placeholders if the workflow relies on consistent branding. Use a representative slide with a dense table and one with a visual diagram. Simple title slides rarely reveal the structural problems that make generated decks costly to maintain.

sections.title: Try next week's sales update
sections.html: Suppose a manager uses an AI deck for a weekly sales meeting. Before accepting it, update the regional totals, add a newly opened territory, and replace a product image. Record the time spent and any layout damage. Check whether the total and explanatory sentence still agree after changing the chart. Then duplicate a slide and apply the standard template. This revision exercise tests the deck's practical reuse, not just its first presentation. If the manager must recreate a chart or rebuild the entire slide to change one number, record that as an editability failure.

sections.title: Check delivery and asset rights
sections.html: Open the file in the intended recipient application and inspect text wrapping, missing fonts, object placement, animations if required, and notes. Export a PDF and compare it with the editable file's visible content. Confirm that images and other assets have an appropriate source and permitted use; generation does not automatically establish rights to every incorporated asset. Review alternative text, color contrast, and reading order according to the audience's accessibility needs. Remove temporary notes, placeholder labels, and unsupported factual claims. A useful acceptance process covers structure, accuracy, accessibility, and distribution together.

sections.title: Object checks by revision task
sections.html:
Next taskInspectCommon obstacle
Update sales figuresEditable values, series, and chart labelsChart is a flat picture
Translate the deckText objects and room for longer labelsText baked into images
Change a process stepManageable shapes, connectors, and groupingDiagram is fragmented or flattened
Apply brandingTheme, fonts, placeholders, and reusable layoutsEvery slide needs manual formatting

For the weekly sales update, change one value that alters a chart label and one territory name that wraps to two lines. Both are ordinary revisions, but they expose different structural weaknesses. Inspect whether related totals and narrative remain consistent, then reopen the deck in the application used by the presenter.

Record limitations precisely. Background photography can reasonably remain an image; a chart reused every week may need editable data. A complex diagram might be acceptable as an image for one final presentation but unsuitable as a reusable template. The acceptance decision should reflect the planned lifecycle, and any regeneration route should preserve approved facts and required assets.

figure.title: Next week's revision is the acceptance test

items.label: Update
items.detail: Change totals, territory labels, and one image.

items.label: Inspect
items.detail: Check layout, calculations, and related commentary.

items.label: Reopen
items.detail: Use the presenter's application and environment.

items.label: Deliver
items.detail: Compare final editable and PDF versions.

figure.alt: An ordinary revision is followed by inspection, reopening, and delivery.
figure.caption: Measure repair work instead of relying only on the first preview.

sections.title: Deck Decision notes record
sections.html:
• List the elements that must remain editable for future work.
  • Inspect text, charts, tables, diagrams, themes, and object grouping.
  • Perform the next expected revision and measure repair effort.
  • Open the file in recipient software and inspect the exported PDF.
  • Review factual claims, assets, notes, and accessibility.

title: AI office work: write a brief that produces reviewable files
description: Specify business outcomes, authoritative context, correction rules, and artifact acceptance for everyday AI tasks.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: OfficeDex: Vibe Officing: AI for Everyday Office Work

intro: A useful AI office brief states the audience, business outcome, deliverables, authoritative sources, and acceptance checks. It should also say what must remain unresolved when evidence is missing. Review the generated files and correct factual rules across every artifact before authorizing distribution.

sections.title: Specify the result and source authority
sections.html:
State who will use the artifact and what decision or action it supports. A request to create a report is incomplete without audience, purpose, scope, and output format. Add required sections, length, tone, and any fixed template or brand requirements. Specify which facts must come from supplied sources and which points should remain open if evidence is missing. Keep technical implementation choices out of the brief unless they affect the result. The authoring tool may choose its own process, but it should not have to guess the business outcome or the standard by which the artifact will be reviewed.

Provide the relevant materials and identify which are current, approved, historical, or tentative. If two sources disagree, name the owner who resolves the conflict or instruct the tool to flag it. Do not bury the essential source among dozens of unrelated attachments. For a numerical task, include units, period, currency, and definitions. For a policy task, distinguish existing policy from proposed changes. These labels reduce the chance that plausible but outdated information enters the output. Use approved data handling arrangements and avoid including sensitive information that the task does not require.

figure.title: The brief should answer the reviewer's questions

items.label: Audience and outcome
items.detail: Who reads the files and what decision they support.

items.label: Inputs
items.detail: Current source versions and their authority.

items.label: Rules
items.detail: Periods, units, exclusions, and unresolved questions.

items.label: Acceptance
items.detail: Observable file checks and distribution approval.

figure.alt: Four brief components make generated office work reviewable.
figure.caption: The tool's technical process is secondary to the accepted business result.

sections.title: Work through a monthly team pack
sections.html:
Imagine a team lead requesting a monthly pack from a staffing workbook and project notes. The brief asks for a one page summary, a staffing table, and four slides for the leadership meeting. It specifies the reporting month, excludes tentative hires from headcount, and requires unresolved project risks to remain visible. After the first draft, the lead notices that a delayed project is described as complete. The correction should point to the source, explain the status rule, and request checks across all three artifacts. Merely asking for better wording would leave the underlying factual problem unresolved.

outcome: leadership understands staffing and project risks
deliverables: one-page summary, staffing table, four slides
period: the nominated reporting month
headcount_rule: exclude tentative hires
source_rule: approved workbook governs numeric totals
review: inspect files and unresolved risks before sending

This is a business brief, not a prescribed implementation stack. Add the actual source versions and the owner who can resolve disputed status. The tool can choose an appropriate drafting process while the reviewer retains a concrete standard for the result.

When the delayed project is described as complete, correct the status rule as well as the sentence. Ask for the summary, table, slide title, and chart annotation to be checked against the same source. Otherwise a local wording repair can leave contradictory artifacts in the pack.

Keep a correction log with the requirement, source evidence, affected artifacts, and verified outcome. Reuse the improved brief next month, but update period and inputs deliberately. A reusable task card should not fossilize last month's assumptions. If the intended audience changes from internal leaders to a customer, reassess confidentiality, terminology, and approval requirements before rerunning it.

sections.title: Review outputs, not confident narration
sections.html: Open every generated file and inspect the parts that matter to the task. Verify totals, source references, tables, page layout, chart labels, and slide structure. Ask whether an ordinary colleague can edit and use the result in the intended application. Record corrections by requirement so the brief improves for the next run. Keep approval and distribution separate from drafting; a tool producing a polished artifact does not establish business authorization to send it. If the tool reports completion while a file is missing or unusable, treat the observable artifact as the authority and repair the workflow.

figure.title: A factual correction must reach every artifact

items.label: Find error
items.detail: Project marked complete contradicts approved notes.

items.label: Correct rule
items.detail: State the source and intended status interpretation.

items.label: Check outputs
items.detail: Inspect summary, table, slides, and repeated labels.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Reviewer accepts identified corrected files.

figure.alt: The correction changes a source rule and is verified across outputs.
figure.caption: Do not treat a repaired sentence as proof that the whole pack is consistent.

sections.title: Reusable task card Decision notes
sections.html:
• Describe audience, decision, deliverables, and required format.
  • Identify authoritative sources, periods, units, and unresolved conflicts.
  • State constraints and facts the tool must not invent.
  • Correct errors with evidence and check every affected artifact.
  • Inspect files and record a human approval before distribution.

title: Steer an AI deck in progress: scope feedback and protect facts
description: Use accepted outlines, versioned comments, bounded revisions, and final consistency checks during deck generation.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: OfficeDex: Steer a deck while it is still drawing

intro: Steer an AI deck by approving its narrative, identifying the draft version under review, and giving bounded feedback that says what to change and preserve. Recheck facts and transitions after each significant revision. Incremental slide approval does not replace review of the complete presentation.

sections.title: Approve a narrative before detail
sections.html: Start with audience, meeting purpose, required conclusion, and the evidence supporting it. Review a short outline before investing in detailed slides. Specify the role of each slide: introduce the problem, show data, explain options, or request a decision. Mark mandatory content and constraints such as a fixed number of slides. The outline becomes a stable reference for later feedback. If the audience or conclusion changes during drafting, acknowledge that as a plan revision rather than applying scattered cosmetic edits to slides built for a different story.

figure.title: Feedback can change evidence, story, or appearance

items.label: Evidence
items.detail: Facts, source versions, and qualifications.

items.label: Narrative
items.detail: Slide purpose, order, and transitions.

items.label: Appearance
items.detail: Layout, chart form, typography, and assets.

items.label: Approval
items.detail: Accepted plan and exact reviewed draft.

figure.alt: Feedback should name the layer being changed.
figure.caption: A visual request should not silently alter accepted evidence.

sections.title: Label provisional work clearly
sections.html: While a deck is being assembled, text, layout, assets, and data may be at different stages of completion. Show or record which parts are provisional so reviewers do not mistake a temporary placeholder for an accepted fact. Use slide identities or clear titles when giving feedback; position numbers can shift as slides are inserted. Identify the generation version to which the comment applies. Without that link, a delayed instruction can overwrite a newer change. Confirm the actual tool's revision and cancellation behavior before relying on interactive steering in a time sensitive workflow.

sections.title: Steer a product review example
sections.html: Suppose a product team is generating six slides for an executive review. After seeing the first two, the owner decides that the audience needs operational risks before feature details. Update the outline and request moving the risk section, while preserving approved figures and customer quotations. Later, the owner asks to simplify one chart rather than regenerate the whole deck. A good revision request names the slide, the required change, and the elements to preserve. After the update, inspect whether the transition to surrounding slides still works. Local improvements can create repetition or gaps in the overall narrative.

sections.title: Bound revisions and verify facts
sections.html: Separate factual corrections, narrative changes, and visual preferences. Factual corrections should trigger checks wherever the same value or claim appears. Narrative changes may require outline revision. Visual changes should normally preserve accepted evidence. Keep a change record for important decisions and stop generation or publication when the underlying requirement becomes unclear. Do not assume a regenerated chart still uses the same numbers, or that a shorter sentence preserves its original qualification. At the final pass, inspect all slides, notes, references, and exports together to detect inconsistencies introduced by incremental feedback.

sections.title: Feedback that changes the right layer
sections.html:
FeedbackLayer affectedFollowup
Lead with operational risksNarrative planRevise outline and transitions
The margin figure is wrongEvidence and repeated claimsCorrect source use throughout the deck
Make this chart simplerVisual representationPreserve values and necessary qualifications
Add a new decision requestPurpose and conclusionCheck whether the accepted plan still fits

A useful instruction might be: On the slide titled Operational risks, replace the crowded chart with the three accepted categories; preserve the values, source date, and qualification in the note. That is more testable than Make it cleaner.

For the executive review, keep the revised outline with the generation version. When a late comment arrives, confirm that it refers to the current slide rather than an earlier draft with the same position number. If the tool cannot apply a bounded change reliably, pause and work from an identified copy. Then inspect adjacent slides and the conclusion. Simplifying one chart can remove the evidence needed for the next slide, while moving a risk section can leave the original introduction repetitive.

figure.title: A bounded revision preserves a reviewable draft

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Name the current version and target slide.

items.label: Request
items.detail: State the change and elements to preserve.

items.label: Apply
items.detail: Create an identified successor or controlled update.

items.label: Inspect
items.detail: Check facts, adjacent slides, and final output.

figure.alt: The revision starts with identification and ends with complete inspection.
figure.caption: Late feedback needs a version relationship to avoid overwriting newer work.

sections.title: Complete-deck Decision notes
sections.html:
• Approve the narrative purpose and slide outline before detailed assembly.
  • Identify provisional content and the version under review.
  • Give scoped feedback with elements to change and preserve.
  • Recheck repeated facts and narrative transitions after revisions.
  • Inspect the complete deck and exported files before approval.

title: AI Word formatting: a pre-send review of the actual file
description: Inspect styles, rendered pages, hidden content, accepted claims, and Word-to-PDF consistency before delivery.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: OfficeDex: AI Word document formatting: A pre-send checklist

intro: Before sending an AI-generated Word document, inspect semantic structure, rendered pages, factual content, and hidden review data. Verify the final file in the recipient's environment and compare any PDF delivery copy. Successful file generation does not prove readable layout or acceptance of the document's commitments.

sections.title: Check structure before appearance
sections.html: Verify that headings use meaningful styles and form a logical hierarchy. Lists should behave as lists, not as manually typed symbols and spaces. Inspect table structure, labels, captions, and links. These properties support navigation, accessibility, and later editing even when the pages already look attractive. Confirm that sections and page breaks are intentional rather than accidental results of repeated blank paragraphs. If the document uses a template, check that generated content follows its required styles and numbering. A document can appear correct in one view while remaining difficult to revise or interpret with assistive technology.

sections.title: Render and inspect every page
sections.html: Open the file in the intended application and inspect a rendered version page by page. Look for clipped text, overlapping objects, split table rows, isolated headings, unexpected blank pages, and inconsistent margins. Check headers, footers, page numbers, and any table of contents after updating fields. Pay special attention to long names, multilingual text, and dense tables because they expose layout weaknesses. Keep the original generated file and a review copy so corrections are traceable. A successful file creation message confirms only that a file exists, not that its rendered output is readable or professionally usable.

figure.title: The final review has four independent dimensions

items.label: Structure
items.detail: Styles, hierarchy, lists, tables, and navigation.

items.label: Rendering
items.detail: Pagination, clipping, overlap, and fields.

items.label: Content
items.detail: Figures, scope, assumptions, and supported claims.

items.label: Disclosure
items.detail: Comments, revisions, metadata, and embedded material.

figure.alt: Four review dimensions cover more than visible formatting.
figure.caption: A neat page cannot compensate for an unsupported commitment.

sections.title: Test a customer proposal
sections.html: Imagine an AI generated proposal containing a scope table, pricing, assumptions, and signature fields. Confirm that the price matches the approved source and that qualifications have not disappeared during summarization. Check whether the scope table continues cleanly across pages and whether each signature label stays with its line. Open the document on a second relevant application or environment if recipient compatibility is important. Export the proposed PDF delivery copy and compare it with the Word file. The recipient should receive the same accepted terms regardless of which supported representation they read.

sections.title: Remove unintended information
sections.html: Inspect comments, tracked changes, document properties, hidden text, embedded objects, and leftover template instructions. Decide which review annotations should be retained and which should be removed before external circulation. Confirm source references and links resolve to the intended materials and do not expose internal resources unnecessarily. Review generated claims for evidence and identify any placeholders or incomplete sections. A formatting pass must not obscure a substantive issue: a neat table containing an invented commitment remains unacceptable. Keep the final approval tied to the exact file version that will be distributed.

sections.title: A page review log catches recurring defects
sections.html:
Use a page review log when the document is substantial or formally delivered. Record page, defect, affected content, correction, and verification. This is more reliable than a general Looks fine comment.

ObservationPossible correction to investigate
Heading isolated at page bottomParagraph keep behavior and section structure
Table text clippedColumn widths, cell margins, and row height rules
Signature label separatedGrouping and intentional page break
Unexpected blank pageSection break, empty paragraph, or layout constraint

Use the editing application's supported controls and verify the rendered result after correction. Changing a font size to fix one page can shift later pages and damage a previously correct table.

sections.title: Keep approval tied to the delivered file
sections.html:
For the proposal, the approval record should identify the file that was actually checked, not merely the project name. If a later regeneration changes pricing, scope, assumptions, or pagination, determine which checks need repeating and obtain the required approval for the successor.

Retain the reviewed Word file and delivered PDF with a clear relationship. If the PDF is the authoritative sent record, label that explicitly. A Word file reopened after a font or field update can render differently, so the delivery check should use the final output rather than an earlier preview. Keep the record concise enough for routine use while preserving the evidence needed to explain what was accepted.

figure.title: Approve the actual delivery artifacts

items.detail: Generated content enters Word review.

items.label: Render
items.detail: Inspect every required page and correct defects.

items.label: Delivery output
items.detail: Create and compare the final PDF if required.

items.label: Approval
items.detail: Identify the accepted versions that will be sent.
